 EDITORIAL: Did we get it wrong while getting it right?
 Published 5:30 am Thursday, November 19, 2026
 Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... 
 It has now been a few of weeks since B.C. stopped the practice of twice annual time changes.
 This was an overwhelmingly popular decision. Sure, as with any change, there were some hiccups. These were primarily logistical and coordination issues related to being out of alignment with neighbouring jurisdictions in the United States.
 But this is something that we’ve always dealt with. While it’s a little unusual to have this alignment issue from north to south, we’ve always been (and will continue to be) out of alignment from east to west. We make it work.
 Within our company, there were some minor technological challenges vis a vis scheduling, but these were quickly resolved and life and business carried on as usual.
 The misalignment should be temporary. Saskatchewan has always been on Central Standard Time year-round. Yukon stopped the practice in 2020. This year, Alberta, Northwest Territories, Manitoba and part of Ontario joined B.C. in adopting permanent Daylight Saving Time.
 There was no sense in waiting for our southern neighbours (Washington, Oregon, California) to jump on the bandwagon. They’ve already passed their own laws to end the time change, but need federal law to catch up before pulling the trigger. They will eventually follow suit.
 This is the way the world is going, we’re just kind of at the leading edge. Kudos to us.
 The only sticking point is why did we (and that includes all the aforementioned Canadian and American jurisdictions) opt for permanent Daylight Saving Time over Standard Time.
 Scientifically, Standard Time was probably the better choice as earlier morning light aligns better with our circadian rhythms. Either way, it’s better than changing twice a year.
 For those of us who live in the northern parts of the province, it’s kind of a moot point. In the winter it’s dark in the morning and the afternoon and in summer it’s light all the time, so six of one, half a dozen of the other.
 And, health experts be damned, having the extra hour of light at the end of the day rather than the beginning was the overwhelming public, business and, therefore, political preference. 
 The argument goes that later sunsets encourage more outdoor recreation, social activity, and local retail and dining patronage after working hours.
 So, here we are. We adjust and we adapt. In a few years, we won’t even remember what it was like back in the old days.
